         Save the Lampasas files these Replies to Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (PFD).

 Pursuant to the Exceptions and Replies Memorandum, filed August 20, 2026, these Replies are

 timely filed on or before September 9, 2026.1

         Save the Lampasas files these replies in response to the Applicants’ and Staff’s

 exceptions to the PFD’s recommendation that the Applicants did not meet their burden of proof

 regarding the need for the Bell County East to Big Hill proposal for Import Path 2.2

 produce evidence on the statutory factors, including need, and that the Commission must make findings on those

                     I.   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF REPLIES

   The Commission should affirm the primary recommendation in the Proposal for Decision
    and deny this application because the Applicants failed to meet their burden of proof to
    show that the line was needed.

   The Commission's approval of Import Path 1 (and presumably Import Path 3) supports
    the PFD’s recommendation for denial in this case for the following reasons:
        o As the record shows, with 55% of the projected load in the Permian Basis
           Reliability Plan (PBRP) being oil and gas load, these two import paths can
           address any short-term need for additional power to the oil and gas loads in the
           Permian Basin that may not be served with new generation.
        o Approval of these two import paths (along with other 345 kV projects that are
           ongoing in the Permian) provides the Commission with time to ensure a properly
           considered analysis of the necessity of some or all of Import Path 2.
        o The evidentiary record here is specific to the study area and impacts of this
           particular project and does not seek to find the PBRP as a whole invalid.

   Even if the Commission determines that the PBRP creates a rebuttable presumption of
    need that has not been refuted, the Commission should acknowledge that under the
    PBRP, the Bell County East to Big Hill project is not needed until at the earliest 2038.


   The PBRP identified projected need in 2038 affords ample time for the Commission to
    follow its own precedent and have ERCOT and the Applicants update the analysis to
    include all new changed conditions – particularly with respect to 45% of the identified
    load related to data centers that the PBRP is designed to serve, and new dispatchable
    generation announcements for generation to be located in the Permian Basin.


   The Application should consider the billions of dollars of transmission line investment
    that the Commission has and will approve for the Permian region to evaluate whether any
    incremental benefits of this proposed project outweigh the permanent alteration of the
    riparian communities that would be traversed under the project as presented here.


   More time would allow the Applicants, ERCOT, and the Commission to incorporate
    consideration of the geography involved to evaluate a starting point that does not put our
    park system and Fort Hood in the center of the routing study area.

      Like Route 894, alternative routes 392, 410, and 487 each rely on links that traverse the
       Lampasas River Valley, including the following impacts affecting the applicable routing
       criteria:
           o Bisecting the Panther Creek Wildlife Management Area (PCWMA);
           o Diagonally bisecting well over 10 miles of family properties in the Lampasas
                River Valley
           o Crossing multiple tributaries of the Lampasas River, including Rocky Creek,
                which is an Ecologically Significant Stream Segment
           o Bisecting multiple adjacent properties with rich historical and archeological
                significance throughout its length that have been preserved, protected, and
                maintained for generations.
           o Traversing an area that is actively used for low-flying helicopter training from
                nearby Fort Hood

      The PFD improperly considers proximity to school as an effective disqualifying factor for
       Route 296, when there are multiple sufficient mitigation options available within the
       record of this case.

      Unlike the prior 765-kV cases considered by this Commission, the PFD in this case did
       not perform a comprehensive routing analysis, and much of the record evidence
       discussed in the PFD on routing supports rejection of Route 894.

      All of the above-identified factors, when considered in the evidentiary record as a whole,
       support selection of Route 296 over Route 894 or any other route.


                             II.    REPLIES TO EXCEPTIONS

       A. Need

Applicable Legal Standards

       The facts of the previous 765-kilovolt (kV) PUC Dockets are distinct from the present

one, and any determinations of need established based on the evidence presented in those

dockets for Import Path 1 (and presumably Import Path 3) are not controlling here. The issue of

need in this matter turns on specific evidence brought forward in this case and also involves a

question of timing.




                                                                                                     005
                                                                                                           Page 5 of 32


       Based on the evidence presented, the Applicants have failed to meet their burden of proof

to demonstrate the need for Import Path 2 and this transmission project. The Commission should

require the Applicants and ERCOT to refresh their analysis of the underlying need for this

project and reconsider the initial starting-point location of Bell County East. This will allow

time to ensure the load projections underlying this project are based on more reliable forecasts

and include only loads forecasted to meet the standards for eligibility for Large Load

interconnections established by the Commission in implementing SB 6.                        Further, the Permian

Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP), which is the cornerstone of need upon which the Applicants rely,

states unambiguously that the need underlying this project is not established until 2038.3

Accordingly, there is ample opportunity to get this right.

       The Applicants seem to have approached this matter as if it were a transmission line to be

approved under the Competitive Renewable Energy Zone (“CREZ”) plan. However, the CREZ

process included a statutory finding of need. Here, no such statutory determination of need

exists. Nor does the Commission Order approving ERCOT’s Permian Basin Reliability Plan

determine need for any of the projects in that plan.4

       Throughout their exceptions, the Applicants characterize the contrary argument and

evidence challenging need as being based on “lay testimony.”5 First, well-reasoned arguments

and references to documentary evidence from the Application itself should not be dismissed just

because they are made by witnesses and parties whose property may be taken as a result of this

proceeding. Second, Save the Lampasas presented expert testimony from the former Chairman

of the Commission, who has extensive familiarity with the transmission line CCN process,

having served as a Commissioner in all CREZ CCN proceedings.

        Even with that statutory determination, the Commission rejected CREZ line applications.

During that process, after hearing the concerns of local property owners and affected

communities, the Commission led an updated analysis and developed alternative solutions.6 This

process led to the cancellation of proposed transmission lines, including the Kendall to Gillespie

and Gillespie to Newton projects, because ERCOT identified alternative solutions that

accomplished the transmission goals without constructing unnecessary infrastructure.7 This

historical precedent demonstrates that the Commission can and should evaluate alternatives that

avoid the permanent destruction of private property and reduce costs for consumers.

        Specific discussions of the evidence are provided below in response to the filed

exceptions that seek to overturn the PFD on this issue.

Load Forecasts and Changed Circumstances

        Rather than presenting evidence of a need study or evaluation for need, the Applicants

defer to ERCOT planning reports; however, those reports do not constitute an analysis sufficient

to meet the Applicants’ burden of proof on need, especially in the face of an evidentiary

challenge to the claimed basis of need for this particular project. For example, the PFD correctly

determined that the evidence shows that the project lacks the capability to perform its reliability

function because the record contains no evidence of surplus generation at the Bell County East

source end of the line.8              While the Commission may consider ERCOT planning

recommendations, it is not bound by ERCOT planning results and must make an independent

legal determination of need based on the evidentiary record in the contested case.                    The

Applicants urge the Commission to reject the PFD because no party presented their own model

unambiguously lies on the Applicants. The Applicants did not present their own model and

instead solely relied on ERCOT’s PBRP.              However, the parties have introduced extensive

evidence supporting the PFD's careful analysis that the plan the Applicants used is out of date

and reflects changed circumstances.

Changed Circumstances and Erroneous Load Forecasts

        The Applicants’ exceptions regarding load forecasts fail to address the PFD’s findings of

changed circumstances because the offered need arguments omit the changed circumstances

regarding the quantification of the non-oil and gas load that constitutes 45% of the projected load

used to support ERCOT’s recommendation of need for the PBRP.                   Under PURA § 37.056(c),

the Commission must consider forecasted load growth to determine if a transmission project is

necessary for public service. Commission Substantive Rule 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II) mandates that

forecasted load growth must be substantiated by quantifiable evidence to support a finding of

need and to receive great weight.

        Under the Commission’s precedent, evaluating necessity requires realistic forecasting to

protect ratepayers from stranded-infrastructure costs. In Project No. 55999, the Commission

approved an adjustment to forecasted loads based on historical analysis of large load realization

rates, applying a 55.4% discount to officer-letter loads and a 49.8% discount to data center

loads.9 The Commission’s order in Project No. 55999 found that good cause existed to

implement these adjustments because of actual experience showing forecasted loads came into

service at lower megawatt levels than transmission service providers claimed.10 Under ERCOT

        Furthermore, former PUC Chairman Barry T. Smitherman testified that the

Commission’s obligation to determine if a line is needed for the convenience and necessity of the

public is distinct from the standard of review of need undertaken at ERCOT.11 As former

Chairman Smitherman testified, while the Commission considers ERCOT’s recommendation, it

is not bound by, and cannot rely solely on the results of the ERCOT process. 12 Former Chairman

Smitherman testified that, to make the appropriate determination of need under the statute, the

Commission should require ERCOT and the applicants to update the analysis when

circumstances change after the initial analysis and plan are issued.13

        The Applicants and Staff both argue in their exceptions that the 2025 Regional

Transmission Plan (RTP) forecasting adjustments are non-retroactive and fail to invalidate the

earlier Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP) recommendations.14 Whether or not the PBRP is

invalidated is not the legal question at issue. The Applicants place undue reliance on the PBRP

as a substitute for a need determination; the Commission’s order approving the PBRP did not

constitute a legal determination of need under PURA § 37.056. The Applicants’ attempt to rely

on the 2025 RTP ignores the factual record showing that officer attestation letters support 55%

of the PBRP’s non-oil and gas load, and 6% remains unconfirmed.15 Applying the Commission-

approved realization rates from Project No. 55999 to these categories results in a reduction of

Bell County East Injection Point

        The Applicants’ exceptions fail to overcome the PFD’s finding that the project lacks the

capability to perform its reliability function because the record contains no evidence of surplus

generation at the Bell County East source end of the line.19 Under PURA § 37.056(a), a utility

seeking a CCN amendment must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the proposed

facilities are necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. For

a transmission line designed to import power into a region, the showing of necessity requires

evidence that the source end has adequate generation to transmit across the line.

        In transmission system planning, a line intended to transmit bulk power to western areas

requires a power surplus at its origin.20 If the origin area is itself experiencing import deficits

and local supply constraints, the proposed line fails to provide the asserted reliability benefits.21

Under ERCOT’s 2023, 2024, and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans, the Central Texas

Corridor, which includes the Bell County area, faces existing import deficits due to lower-rated

345-kV lines.22 The 2025 RTP identifies a need for a new 765-kV import path from Hillje to

Euclid to bring 2,000 MW of power into Central Texas and resolve these local constraints.23

       Chairman Smitherman testified that a consideration influencing his recommendation for

further analysis is that it remains uncertain whether Import Path 2 can deliver new power into the

Permian Basin.24 Chairman Smitherman noted that, unlike the existing and announced generation

at the Comanche Peak facility at the beginning point of Import Path 1 (the proposed Dinosaur

substation), there is no similar announcement for generation capacity at or near the proposed Bell

County East substation.25 He also explained that the Applicants’ focus on the potential benefits

of this project to relieve west-to-east transmission congestion represents a counter-flow argument

that contradicts the characterization of the project as an import path to support operations in the

Permian Basin.26

       The Applicants’ exceptions assert that the ERCOT grid is an interconnected network in

which power flows respond to system conditions on a system-wide basis, making specific

generator identification unnecessary.27 This argument fails to address the factual deficiency

regarding the Central Texas region’s net generation position.28 As the evidence reflects, the

Applicants admitted that neither they nor ERCOT studied Central Texas’s net generation

position under current conditions, projected 2030 conditions, or scenarios assuming data center

Timing of Need

         Even based on inflated non-oil and gas load projections, the PBRP indicates that Import

Path 2 would not be needed until 2038.31                To counter this aspect of the PBRP, the Applicants

brought in a rebuttal witness to introduce assertions regarding Far West Texas import Generic

Transmission Constraints supported by ERCOT market notices.32

         The Applicants’ exceptions attempting to rely on these post-PBRP actions fail to address

the PFD’s finding of a lack of standalone need because it omitted a partial build study to evaluate

Import Path 2 as an independent project. As indicated in the Applicants’ exceptions, the PBRP is

a complex set of transmission upgrades, many of which the Commission has approved and that

are underway.33 In addition, the Commission has approved Import Path 1, and it is reasonable to

presume that Import Path 3 is likely to receive similar approval. The market notices on which

the Applicants rely for these new GTC’s do not provide a sufficient analysis to conclude that the

            Under PURA § 37.056, the Commission must evaluate the need for each proposed

transmission line on an individual basis to determine if it stands on its own merit. System-wide

regional planning guidelines fail to substitute for proof of project-specific need for a single

proposed line. In CCN proceedings, a utility seeking to amend its certificate for a major

transmission expansion must establish that the proposed project for which authority to construct

is being requested is necessary. Chairman Smitherman testified that because of this statutory

distinction, the Commission must vet the project’s incremental need and timing rather than take

time to evaluate alternatives to permanently altering the land.35 Even if the Commission gives

great weight to ERCOT's PBRP recommendations, it is not bound by ERCOT planning results

and must make an independent legal determination of need based on the evidentiary record in the

contested case.

            In their exceptions, the Applicants argue that the PBRP is an integrated reliability plan

individual line.37 The record shows that ERCOT’s own sequencing study prioritized the northern

and southern import paths over central Import Path 2, indicating that the immediate need for this

specific segment is unproven.38 The Applicants’ reliance on NERC TPL-001 N-1-1

New Generation Announcement Should be Considered

       The Applicants’ exceptions fail to address the PFD’s finding that local generation

alternatives reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2 because the arguments fail to rebut

the existence of 25.162 GW of planned or active gas generation in the Permian Basin. PURA §

37.056(c) requires that a proposed transmission project must be compared to alternative

solutions, which include local generation development, to determine the most cost-effective and

reliable plan for ratepayers.

       In evaluating whether a new transmission line is necessary, the Commission considers

whether developing generation closer to the load center provides a superior alternative to

constructing thousands of miles of high-voltage transmission lines.40 Former Chairman

Smitherman testified that during the CREZ process, after hearing the concerns of local property

owners and affected communities, the Commission led an updated analysis and developed

alternative solutions.41 This process led to the cancellation of proposed transmission lines,

including the Kendall to Gillespie and Gillespie to Newton projects, because ERCOT identified

       B. Routing Criteria

       Save the Lampasas files these replies to exceptions in response to the following groups:

J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners, Solana Intervenors, Brady Creek Intervenors, Staten Creek

Ranch, and 4K Land and Cattle Company to the extent that they support a route that contains

G51/G52 if the Commission approves the application. The discussion of the record presented by

these and other parties establishes that Route 894 should not be approved if the Commission

moves forward with selecting a route. Route 894 performs poorly on environmental metrics,

relies on problematic Colorado River crossing close to Post Oak Ridge State Park, generates

significant landowner opposition (i.e., proponents of 392, 487, and 296 all opposed 894), and

inadequately accounts for impacts to state parks, historic ranches, and community values.

Although some intervenors contend that Routes 392 and 487 perform better than Route 894, that

comparison only reinforces why Route 894 is deficient overall. Routes 392 and 487, and others

discussed in the exceptions, merely transfer the same negative historical, environmental,

community, recreational, and ranching impacts to other affected landowners and do not provide

the balanced outcome required by the statutory routing factors. If it approves the Application,

the Commission should therefore select Route 296 and reject Routes 392, 487, and 894.

to exceptions focus primarily on arguments supporting other routes raised in filed exceptions that
